verses.1: Al-Mizan describes this Meccan sūrah as warning doubters of the clear Book of worldly and final punishment, illustrated by Pharaoh’s people and then by the Resurrection, hell, and the Godwary’s reward. The Manifest Book is the Qur’an, sent on the blessed Night of Ordainment, a recurring night in Ramadan. The Qur’an descended as a whole on that night and also gradually over the twenty-three-year mission, but not in the same individuated form: its event-bound verses make identical simultaneous and gradual revelation impossible. The first descent must therefore be general versus detailed, or, more precisely, God made the Prophet fully aware when revelation reached elaboration in the Divine Decree before particular earthly occurrences. The alternative that gradual revelation merely began that night contradicts the verses’ apparent meaning; the report of descent first to the lowest heaven rests on transmitted traditions. ‘Every definitive matter is separated’ concerns continuous passage in the Divine Decree from an undifferentiated, ḥakīm state to specified cosmic determination, including the Qur’an; it is not a continuing elaboration of Qur’anic laws. The Book’s descent is an affair or command from God and a mercy from the Prophet’s Lord, who hears needs and knows them. He is not a private Lord but Lord of all heavens, earth, and what lies between; those with conviction know this. His sole lordship entails His sole divinity, while giving life and death prepares the warning of return, and His lordship over forefathers removes ancestral imitation as an excuse.

verses.3: Al-Mizan identifies the blessed night as the Night of Ordainment, recurring each lunar Ramadan and rich in mercy. It holds that the entire Qur’an was sent down then as well as gradually through the mission, but rejects an identical double descent because verses are tied to particular events. It accordingly distinguishes a general and a detailed descent, or says the Prophet was made aware of the fully elaborated Qur’an in the Decree before its particular revelations. The claim that only gradual revelation began that night contradicts the apparent wording; descent first to the lowest heaven is reported from traditions. ‘We have been warning’ shows that warning through prophets and revelation is God’s continuing custom, not a novelty.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says the Night of Ordainment is where every ḥakīm, undifferentiated matter is continuously separated and specified. Divine Decree thus has a general stage and an elaborated stage, and the Qur’an is among what descends through that separation. It proposes that God informed the Prophet of future events and their accompanying revelations at this stage. The reading that the verse continuously elaborates Qur’anic teachings is rejected because the imperfect verb indicates an ongoing process, which fits cosmic determination, not a completed Book; the alternative that ḥakīm means made unchangeable after separation is less apparent.
verses.5: Al-Mizan allows amr to qualify the preceding matter as an affair originating from God, or to mean that every matter is separated by His command. It can alternatively modify the Book’s descent: the Book is an affair from God or descends by His command. ‘We have been sending’ then explains that revelation follows His continuing practice of sending messengers. Its descent is mercy from the Prophet’s Lord, who hears what people ask and knows their need for guidance. Calling Him Lord of all heavens, earth, and what lies between refutes any notion that He is merely the Prophet’s private Lord; ‘should you have conviction’ means this is what people of conviction know.

verses.8: Al-Mizan says exclusive lordship over all creation entails exclusive ulūhiyyah, worthiness of worship, so the profession of divine unity excludes every other deity. Giving life and death are distinctive acts of governance and prepare for resurrection. Naming Him the audience’s Lord and the Lord of their forefathers directly removes ancestral imitation as a defense of idolatry; both clauses predicate an implicit ‘It is He.’
verses.9: Al-Mizan says the Prophet’s people lack conviction in the Book and message and, rather than responding, remain absorbed in worldly preoccupations while playing in doubt. It notes Zamakhsharī’s linkage of ‘rather’ to ‘should you have conviction’ (44:7).
verses.10: Al-Mizan calls the smoke a warning of punishment but reports conflicting identifications. One is the Meccan famine invoked by the Prophet, in which starvation made people see smoke and they ate carrion and bones before breaking their pledge when relief came. Another is a future sign of the Hour lasting forty days and afflicting believers and unbelievers differently. Identifying it with the dust of Mecca’s conquest or with resurrection is also possible, but these are as they appear. The smoke envelops the Meccans on the first reading and all people on the second.

verses.12: Al-Mizan says that when the punishment of Smoke comes, people call it painful and ask God to remove it, professing belief in His true religion and lordship.
verses.13: Al-Mizan rejects their profession as insincere: a manifest Messenger, Muḥammad, had already brought an undeniable message, yet they turned from him and called him a ‘tutored madman’—both accusing him of human instruction despite his attribution to God and of lost reason.
verses.14: Al-Mizan rejects their profession as insincere: a manifest Messenger, Muḥammad, had already brought an undeniable message, yet they turned from him and called him a ‘tutored madman’—both accusing him of human instruction despite his attribution to God and of lost reason.
verses.15: Al-Mizan says that on the Meccan-famine reading God briefly removes the punishment, while knowing they will revert to disbelief and denial. On the universal-resurrection reading, their return is to punishment on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.16: Al-Mizan reports the ‘most terrible striking’ as Badr on the famine reading or the Day of Resurrection on the other. It gives the latter weight because God’s punishment, as well as His reward, is greatest in the Hereafter.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says fitnah is a test revealing people’s true state, here effected by the coming of Moses. Calling him karīm describes manifest virtuous character; the term changes by subject, naming God’s generosity, a human’s praiseworthy conduct, and whatever is noble in its kind.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says Moses’ message ordered Pharaoh to release the Israelites, called God’s servants to awaken mercy and to show that oppressing them aggresses against God. By calling himself a trusted Messenger he denies that freeing them conceals a plan to expel Egyptians. It rejects the alternative that ‘servants of God’ addresses Pharaoh and his people directly, since it does not fit the apparent wording.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes Moses’ prohibition as forbidding arrogant denial of God’s message, since denying a Messenger defies his Sender. His manifest authority consists of irrefutable miracles and sound argument; the pairing of ‘deliver/trusted’ and ‘defy/authority’ is noted as eloquent.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says Moses seeks protection from his and their Lord against stoning, relying on God’s prior assurance that Pharaoh’s people could not harm him. It therefore rejects the view that he spoke before receiving that assurance.
verses.21: Al-Mizan reads Moses’ words as: if they will not believe, they should keep away without benefiting or harming him. The proposed sense of cutting themselves off from him is less likely.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says Moses invoked God by declaring them a guilty people whose transgression deserved destruction; God’s command to set out by night supplies the answer to that prayer.
verses.23: Al-Mizan notes that isrāʾ already means night travel, so ‘by night’ reinforces it. God’s servants are the Israelites, and the concise prediction tells Moses that Pharaoh and his army will pursue them.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes ‘leave the sea calm’ as leaving it open as a wide path, rather than closing it. The verse compactly implies the crossing after Moses strikes the sea, then Pharaoh’s army entering the path and drowning; their drowning is the reason for leaving it so.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says ‘how many’ magnifies the gardens, springs, fields, noble residences, and enjoyments Pharaoh’s people left behind. Noble places are beautiful, lavish abodes; their delight may mean convivial speech or enjoyment of fruit.

verses.28: Al-Mizan reports several possibilities for kadhālik—‘the affair was thus,’ God’s habitual ruin of a people, the preceding manner of bringing them out, or a qualifier of what they left. In all cases, their gardens and possessions were bequeathed to another people.
verses.29: Al-Mizan treats heaven and earth not weeping as a figurative declaration of Pharaoh’s people’s cosmic insignificance. Their immediate destruction and lack of respite show that no protection or means could avert the divine decree.
verses.30: Al-Mizan identifies the humiliating torment as Pharaoh’s oppression of Israel, including killing their sons and sparing women. ‘From Pharaoh’ may identify its perpetrator or hyperbolically make Pharaoh himself the torment; he was tyrannical even among the profligate.
verses.31: Al-Mizan identifies the humiliating torment as Pharaoh’s oppression of Israel, including killing their sons and sparing women. ‘From Pharaoh’ may identify its perpetrator or hyperbolically make Pharaoh himself the torment; he was tyrannical even among the profligate.
verses.32: Al-Mizan says God chose Israel knowingly because they merited selection. ‘Above all worlds’ means all nations in particular respects, such as their many prophets and exceptional signs, or, if categorical, only the people of their own time, not the Muslim community.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says Israel’s miraculous signs were manifest tests. The story’s conclusion also consoles the Prophet and hints that God will save him and believers from Mecca’s Pharaohs, establish them, and then test their conduct.
verses.34: Al-Mizan says Quraysh deny postmortem life and resurrection by making the first death their final end. It reports four explanations: ordinary first death followed by no further life; a reply to the promise of a death followed by life; most plausibly, denial of the second death after barzakh because they take death for annihilation; or God’s explanatory designation rather than their own word. It ranks the third closest, then the fourth and first.

verses.36: Al-Mizan says the deniers challenge the Prophet and believers to revive their dead fathers, treating such a return as proof that death is not annihilation and resurrection true.
verses.37: Al-Mizan makes the people of Tubbaʿ and earlier guilty communities a threat to the present deniers: God destroyed them and can destroy these. Tubbaʿ was a Ḥimyarite king in Yemen, and the wording hints that he himself was spared.
verses.38: Al-Mizan says creation ‘with truth’ means creation accompanied by truth, not merely caused by faith, obedience, resurrection, and recompense. It derives resurrection rationally: if this changing material world had no enduring destination beyond it, repeated creation and death would be pointless play, impossible for God whose acts have ends. This world must therefore lead to the lasting Hereafter; their ignorance merits rebuke.

verses.40: Al-Mizan calls the Resurrection the Day of Separation because God decisively separates truth from falsehood, their people, and the Godwary from the guilty. It is the appointed meeting for all people, including the peoples just mentioned.
verses.41: Al-Mizan distinguishes a mawlā who can avail another unilaterally from a helper who supplements the other’s insufficient means. Neither operates on that Day because worldly recourses are cut off. The exception ‘except whom God has mercy’ most naturally establishes intercession, if ‘they’ means people generally; if it means unbelievers, it is discontinuous and the Godwary need no help. A continuous exception to mawlā is rejected because intercession itself requires a recipient’s valid means of salvation, namely a God-approved religion. God’s might means none can prevent His punishment, and His mercy means He gives goodness as He wills.

verses.43: Al-Mizan says the tree of Zaqqūm, already discussed elsewhere, is food for the athīm, one in whom sin inheres through abundance or persistence. The surrounding verses describe hell’s inhabitants.
verses.44: Al-Mizan says the tree of Zaqqūm, already discussed elsewhere, is food for the athīm, one in whom sin inheres through abundance or persistence. The surrounding verses describe hell’s inhabitants.
verses.45: Al-Mizan identifies muhl as molten copper, perhaps other melted metal, and ḥamīm as intensely hot water. Zaqqūm is successively described as the sinners’ food, like molten metal, and boiling in their bellies like boiling water.

verses.47: Al-Mizan says the angels of hell are ordered to seize the sinner and drag him violently into hell’s middle so that it surrounds him, then pour over his head boiling water used as punishment.
verses.48: Al-Mizan says the angels of hell are ordered to seize the sinner and drag him violently into hell’s middle so that it surrounds him, then pour over his head boiling water used as punishment.
verses.49: Al-Mizan says calling the suffering sinner mighty and noble is mockery that intensifies punishment, contrasting his abasement with the worldly self-regard in which he assumed he would have the best with God.
verses.50: Al-Mizan says this both reinforces their punishment and exposes their worldly doubt by making them taste what they doubted. It is also possible that the plural address begins a new speech to Qur’anic hearers rather than continuing the singular sinner’s punishment.
verses.51: Al-Mizan says the Godwary’s secure station is a place safe from all harm, namely gardens and springs. They wear fine silk and brocade and sit face-to-face in affability, without the evil or hurt that would disturb that security.

verses.54: Al-Mizan says they are made partners to ḥūr al-ʿīn; tazwīj originally means pairing. Ḥūr denotes intensely contrasted or black eyes, and ʿīn large eyes. These houris are apparently distinct from the believing women of this world who enter Paradise.
verses.55: Al-Mizan says their calling for every fruit is in complete safety from any harmful effect of it.
verses.56: Al-Mizan says Paradise entails eternal life and protection from hell. To resolve ‘they will not taste death except the first death,’ it prefers a discontinuous exception: they tasted worldly death and it has passed; alternatively illā means ‘other than’ without a true exception. It then accounts for the two deaths—worldly death into barzakh and barzakh’s end—by reading the wording to deny any death in Paradise, while the first has already occurred. Guarding against hell together with deathlessness covers both transition from bliss and transition into misery. These blessings are grace, not an earned claim upon God, though His promise is true; this is the supreme success.

verses.58: Al-Mizan treats this as the sūrah’s conclusion: God made the Book easy in the Prophet’s Arabic tongue so that his people might grasp its purposes and take admonition. It rejects the reading that ease means merely the illiterate Prophet’s recitation, which does not fit this summation.
verses.59: Al-Mizan says that because they neither take admonition nor cease playing in doubt, the Prophet is to await their unavoidable punishment while they derisively await it too. It rejects the claim that this command was abrogated by the Sword Verse.
